question.text: Mrs. Gupta, an eligible and certified new cadre distributor, wants to recommend a mutual fund scheme to a conservative client. The scheme's benchmark is Nifty 50, and the scheme's returns for the last 3 years were: Year 1: 12% (Nifty: 10%), Year 2: 8% (Nifty: 9%), Year 3: 15% (Nifty: 14%). Can she sell this scheme as a new cadre distributor?

answer.text: Yes, because the overall 3-year return is higher than Nifty
No, because the scheme underperformed its benchmark in Year 2
Yes, because 2 out of 3 years had better returns
No, because only index funds can be sold

explanation.text: The Logic: For new cadre distributors, eligible products must have returns equal to or better than the scheme benchmark in EACH of the last three years — not on average. In Year 2 the scheme returned 8% while the Nifty 50 returned 9%, so the scheme fails the year-by-year benchmark test and is not eligible for sale. The Trap: Averaging or summing the 3-year returns makes the scheme look acceptable, but the rule is per-year. "2 out of 3 years" still fails the test. "Only index funds can be sold" misstates the new cadre eligibility framework. Note: Stem rewritten to describe Mrs. Gupta as an eligible and certified new cadre distributor, removing the retired-teacher qualification ambiguity.
